title: Electron shells, valence electrons and the periodic table
blurb: Fill electron shells, count valence electrons and use them to place any of the first 20 elements on the periodic table.
question: Phosphorus has atomic number 15. Without looking at a periodic table, how many valence electrons does it have, which period is it in, and is it more likely to gain or lose electrons?

teach.body: Formally, electrons occupy energy levels (shells) around the nucleus, numbered 1, 2, 3 outward, each holding up to 2n² electrons. In plain English: shells are like floors of a building that fill from the ground up. Shell 1 holds 2, shell 2 holds 8, and for the first 20 elements shell 3 takes 8 before shell 4 starts, giving the pattern 2, 8, 8, 2.

head: Shell (n)
2n²
First 20 elements
teach.caption: Inside each shell are sublevels: s holds 2, p holds 6, d holds 10, f holds 14. Oxygen is 1s² 2s² 2p⁴.

head: Element (Z)
Shells
Valence e⁻
teach.caption: The last number in the arrangement is the valence count. The number of shells used is the period.

teach.body: Valence electrons are the electrons in the outermost shell, and they decide how an atom bonds and how reactive it is. The octet rule: atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons to reach 8 valence electrons, the stable arrangement of a noble gas (helium is stable with 2). Electrons that absorb energy jump to higher levels and give out light as they fall back, which is why elements show flame colors.

teach.caption: For groups 13 to 18, drop the 1: group 15 has 5 valence electrons. Transition metals (groups 3 to 12) do not follow this shortcut.

teach.body: The modern periodic table lists elements by increasing atomic number (Moseley). Mendeleev's first table used atomic mass and left gaps for elements he correctly predicted. Periods are the 7 horizontal rows: the period number equals the number of occupied shells. Groups (families) are the 18 vertical columns: members share the same number of valence electrons, so they have similar chemical properties.

children.label: B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te

teach.body: Priya, a nursing applicant, gets a practice item on phosphorus (Z = 15). She fills shells: 2, 8, 5. Three shells means period 3. Five valence electrons means group 15. Phosphorus sits to the upper right, so it is a nonmetal, and with 5 valence electrons it reaches an octet more easily by gaining 3 electrons than by losing 5.

teach.text: Groups (columns) share properties; periods (rows) share only the number of shells. And watch the symbols: Na is sodium, K is potassium, Fe iron, Cu copper, Ag silver, Au gold, Pb lead, Hg mercury, Sn tin.

items: Shells fill from the inside: 2, then 8, then 8, then 2 for the first 20 elements.
Valence electrons are in the outermost shell and control bonding; atoms aim for an octet.
Period number = number of occupied shells. Group = valence electrons (group 1 = 1, group 17 = 7).
The modern table is ordered by atomic number; Mendeleev used atomic mass.
Metals lose electrons (cations); nonmetals gain or share them; metalloids are semiconductors.

summary: You can now write the shell arrangement of the first 20 elements, count valence electrons and use them to find an element's period and group. You can also predict whether an element is a metal, nonmetal or metalloid and whether it tends to gain or lose electrons.

A.q: What is the maximum number of electrons the second shell (n = 2) can hold?
A.why: Capacity is 2n². For n = 2, that is 2 × 2² = 8.

whyNot.0: 2 is the capacity of the first shell (n = 1).
whyNot.1: 6 is the capacity of a p sublevel, not of the whole second shell (which also has an s sublevel).
whyNot.3: 18 is the capacity of the third shell (n = 3).

A.q: Calcium has atomic number 20. How are its electrons arranged in shells?
A.why: For the first 20 elements, the third shell takes 8 before the fourth starts: 2 + 8 + 8 + 2 = 20.

whyNot.0: Although shell 3 can eventually hold 18, it takes 8 before shell 4 begins in the first 20 elements.
whyNot.2: The second shell holds a maximum of 8, so 18 cannot sit there.
whyNot.3: Shell 3 stops at 8 for these elements; 9 breaks the 2, 8, 8, 2 pattern.

A.q: Elements in the same group of the periodic table share which feature?
options: Equal numbers of neutrons in the nucleus
A.why: A group (column) shares the same valence electron count, which gives its members similar chemical properties.

whyNot.0: Elements in the same period (row) share the number of shells.
whyNot.1: Atomic mass rises steeply going down a group.
whyNot.2: Neutron counts vary between elements and even between isotopes; they do not define a group.

B.q: How many valence electrons does a chlorine atom (atomic number 17) have?
B.why: Chlorine's arrangement is 2, 8, 7: seven electrons in the outer shell (group 17).

whyNot.1: 8 is the octet chlorine reaches after gaining an electron (as Cl⁻), not what the atom has.
whyNot.2: 1 valence electron belongs to group 1 elements such as sodium.
whyNot.3: 17 is the total electron count, not the outer-shell count.

B.q: Which property is typical of a nonmetal?
options: Tends to lose electrons in bonding
B.why: Nonmetals are dull, brittle when solid and poor conductors, and they gain or share electrons.

whyNot.0: Malleability and ductility are properties of metals.
whyNot.1: Metals conduct well; nonmetals are insulators.
whyNot.3: Losing electrons to form cations is typical of metals; nonmetals gain or share them.

B.q: An element's atoms have exactly three occupied electron shells. Where on the periodic table does that place it?
B.why: The period number equals the number of occupied shells, so three shells means period 3.

whyNot.0: Period 2 elements have two occupied shells.
whyNot.2: Groups reflect valence electrons, not the number of shells.
whyNot.3: Group 13 means 3 valence electrons; this stem gives the number of shells.

C.q: Element X has atomic number 15. Which statement about X is correct?
options: It is in period 2 with 5 valence electrons
It is in period 3 with 3 valence electrons
It is in period 5 with 3 occupied shells
It is in period 3 with 5 valence electrons
C.why: 15 electrons fill as 2, 8, 5: three shells (period 3) and five valence electrons (group 15).

whyNot.0: Two shells hold only 10 electrons, so 15 electrons need a third shell: period 3.
whyNot.1: The outer shell holds 15 − 10 = 5 electrons, not 3.
whyNot.2: The period is the number of shells (3), not the number of valence electrons.

C.q: Lithium, sodium and potassium all react vigorously with water. Which feature of their electron arrangement explains this shared behavior?
options: Two electrons in the outer shell
C.why: All three are in group 1 with one valence electron, which they lose easily; same group, similar chemistry.

whyNot.1: They have 2, 3 and 4 shells respectively, so the shell count is not shared.
whyNot.2: A full octet makes an element unreactive (the noble gases).
whyNot.3: Two outer electrons describe group 2, the alkaline earth metals.

C.q: Mendeleev's first periodic table differed from the modern table because it ordered the elements by:
C.why: Mendeleev arranged elements by atomic mass and left gaps for undiscovered elements; Moseley later reordered by atomic number.

whyNot.0: Increasing atomic number is the modern ordering (Moseley), not Mendeleev's.
whyNot.1: Valence electrons explain the groups, but electrons were not known when Mendeleev built his table.
whyNot.3: Shell counts explain the periods, but they were not the basis of Mendeleev's ordering.

reteach.title: An apartment building for electrons
reteach.question: Imagine every atom as an apartment building whose floors fill from the ground up. How do the floors explain periods, groups and reactivity?

blocks.body: The ground floor has room for 2 residents, the next floor 8, the third 8 (for the first 20 elements). New residents always take the lowest free floor. The number of floors in use is the period. The people on the top occupied floor are the valence electrons: they meet the neighbors, so they decide how the building interacts. A building with a full top floor (8) is content and keeps to itself: a noble gas.

blocks.text: Count floors for the PERIOD and top-floor residents for the GROUP. Mixing them up is the most common placement error.

explain.body: Electrons fill the lowest shell first. Capacity is 2n², but for the first 20 elements the order is 2, then 8, then 8, then 2. Add up to the atomic number.

test.q: Sodium has atomic number 11. What is its shell arrangement?
test.why: Fill from the inside: 2 in shell 1, 8 in shell 2, and the last 1 in shell 3.

whyNot.0: Shell 2 holds a maximum of 8, so the ninth electron must start shell 3.
whyNot.2: The first shell holds only 2, so it cannot hold 8.
whyNot.3: Shells fill in order; shell 2 must be full (8) before shell 3 receives electrons.

explain.h: Valence electrons and the octet rule
explain.body: Valence electrons sit in the outer shell. Atoms gain, lose or share electrons to reach 8 (a noble-gas arrangement). Atoms with 1 to 3 tend to lose them; atoms with 5 to 7 tend to gain.

test.q: An oxygen atom has the arrangement 2, 6. How does it most easily reach a stable octet?
test.why: With 6 valence electrons, oxygen needs only 2 more to reach 8, forming O²⁻.

whyNot.0: Losing six electrons takes far more energy than gaining two; nonmetals gain electrons.
whyNot.1: Losing two would leave 4 in the outer shell, not an octet.
whyNot.2: Gaining six would give 12 outer electrons, overshooting the octet.

explain.body: Rows are periods (7): the number of occupied shells. Columns are groups (18): the number of valence electrons, so members behave alike. The table is ordered by atomic number.

test.q: Which statement about the layout of the periodic table is correct?
options: Rows are periods; columns are groups
Rows are groups; columns are periods
Columns share the same number of shells
test.why: Horizontal rows are periods and vertical columns are groups; groups share valence electrons and chemistry.

whyNot.1: This reverses the terms: groups are the vertical columns.
whyNot.2: Similar chemical properties run down columns (groups), not across rows.
whyNot.3: Elements in a row (period) share the shell count; columns share valence electrons.

explain.body: Metals (left and center) are shiny, malleable, ductile conductors that lose electrons. Nonmetals (upper right, plus hydrogen) are dull, brittle insulators that gain or share electrons. Metalloids line the staircase between them and are semiconductors.

items.label: B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te

test.q: Silicon is used in computer chips because it is a semiconductor. Which category does silicon belong to?
test.why: Silicon sits on the staircase line and has intermediate properties: it is a metalloid.

whyNot.0: Transition metals are in groups 3 to 12 and are good conductors, not semiconductors.
whyNot.1: Nonmetals are insulators; silicon's semiconducting behavior marks it as a metalloid.
whyNot.3: Alkaline earth metals are group 2 (Be, Mg, Ca); silicon is in group 14.
